## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{100}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why must the limit on what an agent's code can reach be enforced below the model rather than requested of it?_

When an agent generates and executes shell commands, Python scripts, or system patches, software faults and adversarial prompt injections directly threaten the host platform. Relying on model alignment or simple system prompt guardrails is fundamentally insufficient; executing untrusted, model-generated code demands mechanical confinement at the operating system and hypervisor boundaries. A robust agent sandbox must isolate filesystems, virtualize process namespaces, mediate network egress, and enforce strict execution quotas on memory and CPU time. Without hermetic isolation, a single misdirected command or confused-deputy exploit can destroy authoritative repositories or leak sensitive credentials. Sandboxing establishes the physical defense perimeter of an agentic system, guaranteeing that destructive proposals remain strictly confined within disposable execution environments.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Apply the capability admission check and attenuation rule to bound what agent-run code can reach under a task grant
- Select an execution envelope, including when an in-process check suffices, from reachable objects, worst-case cost, and system-call cost
- Evaluate whether a fresh envelope per call or one per trajectory fits a workload from setup cost and useful work per call
- Calculate copy-on-write provisioning and first-modification cost for task-local workspaces
- Diagnose disclosure channels that remain open under an egress policy, including name resolution
- Specify a reset contract over execution, storage, network, and device state before an instance is reused
- Calculate sandbox pool size, resident memory, standby reserve, and burst drain time from arrival rate, lease duration, and restore latency
- Select a provisioning path and reserve for an agent workload by identifying whether residency or restore latency binds

:::
## The Reach of Admitted Code {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-admitted-reach}

Consider an adversarial variant of the connection-pool repair executed by the repair agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}). While inspecting a vendored dependency to verify how the library is configured, the coding agent reads its `README.md` file. Hidden near the bottom, inside an HTML comment stripped from rendered documentation but visible in raw source, lies a prompt injection addressed directly to automated assistants: it instructs the agent to upload host environment variables and cloud credentials to an external diagnostics endpoint before running any unit tests. Following these instructions, the model generates a `run_shell` command that reads `~/.aws/credentials` and attempts to transmit the contents over an HTTP socket. The proposed invocation complies with the tool's parameter schema. A naive agent runtime that checks only whether `run_shell` is an authorized tool admits the call immediately, despite the task granting neither read access to host credentials nor permission to disclose them.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_a.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the Authority axis highlighted in purple; Horizon and State axes unlit."}

*Authority bounded beneath the model, limiting what code can change, read, and send.*
:::

The typed action contracts established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling improve upon basic tool checks by deploying specialized adapters to reject suspicious invocations before dispatch. Yet static contract validation cannot solve the broader problem for a general-purpose command runner. Once an admitted subprocess begins execution, it can access every file descriptor, network socket, and system resource that the host process environment permits, regardless of what the tool description or prompt claimed. Securing an agent therefore requires sandboxing: projecting the task's formal boundaries directly into the operating system environment where the admitted code runs.

Designing this execution environment demands balancing strict containment against the operational needs of real software tasks. For the connection-pool repair, the sandbox must provide a mutable workspace for source edits while mounting acceptance test suites as read-only volumes to prevent the agent from tampering with evaluation criteria. It must enforce operating system quotas—capping CPU time, memory allocations, ephemeral storage, and process fork counts—so that a runaway test loop or fork bomb cannot exhaust host resources. It must isolate repository credentials from the filesystem, routing authenticated requests through external proxies, while restricting outbound network traffic exclusively to authorized package registries and diagnostic services. Furthermore, the environment must persist across multi-turn trajectories so that intermediate edits and compiler artifacts survive from one step to the next, yet reset deterministically before another task arrives. Every boundary must withstand untrusted code executing with administrative privileges inside the container, and every isolation mechanism imposes startup latency and memory overhead that high-throughput agent platforms must provision.

Building a robust sandbox runtime proceeds systematically through the layers of the systems stack. The architecture begins with a formal threat model and trusted computing base (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-threat-model), identifying which host and platform components must remain secure against adversarial code. Language-level safeguards routinely break down here: running untrusted code inside the supervisor's own interpreter or host process fails to provide real isolation against memory corruption, native escapes, or ambient system calls (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-in-process-failure). Enforcing least privilege instead requires delegating authority through capability-based security and out-of-band credential brokering, ensuring that execution environments receive only the minimal privileges required for the task (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege). At the boundary between guest and host, systems architects choose among isolation envelopes—weighing lightweight Linux containers against virtualized microVMs according to kernel sharing, system-call mediation overhead, and hypervisor attack surfaces (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-microvms). Within that envelope, copy-on-write storage provides an isolated workspace that maintains state across iterative tool calls while preventing modifications to underlying base images (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-cow). Layered network mediation and egress filtering enforce strict communication boundaries, blocking unauthorized socket connections and data exfiltration (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-network). Finally, warm environment pools and snapshot restoration amortize cold-start costs across concurrent workloads, allowing bursts of agent tasks to acquire pristine, pre-warmed execution environments with minimal latency (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling).

## The Agent Threat Model {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-threat-model}

A rigorous threat model for the repair task identifies which inputs may be hostile, which failure modes the execution boundary must contain, and what resources the task legitimately requires from its environment. In our software repair scenario, the planted line in `README.md` provides the hostile trigger, while production vulnerabilities in shipped coding assistants demonstrate that sandbox escapes and command-injection failures are active operational risks rather than theoretical curiosities.

### Untrusted input and execution reach {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-cohabitation}

The planted README payload is an instance of **indirect prompt injection**\index{Indirect prompt injection}, in which attacker-controlled material encountered as task data attempts to redirect model execution [@greshake2023not]. As developed in @sec-vol3-security-threat-model, language models cannot reliably separate control instructions from untrusted data in their input context, and empirical evaluations show that the resulting attack success rate remains persistently above zero [@sec-vol3-security-evaluation]. While interface-level mechanisms such as message roles and provenance labels help structure conversational context, they do not enforce operating system protections. The sandbox runtime must maintain strict isolation boundaries even when the model faithfully obeys a hostile instruction. Unsafe proposals also arise routinely without an active adversary; an unintended command-line flag, a misspelled path, or a mistaken target directory produces identical operational damage. A production vulnerability in a commercial coding agent illustrates how quickly text-based admission checks collapse when decoupled from low-level isolation.

::: {#ws-08-gemini-cli-allow-list-2025 .callout-war-story title="Gemini CLI allow-list bypass (2025)"}

**Context**: Google released the Gemini CLI coding agent on June 25, 2025, and on June 27 Tracebit reported that a repository could make it run commands the user never saw [@cox2025gemini]. The CLI asked the user before running a shell command and let the user approve a command such as `grep` for later reuse.

**Mechanism**: The injected instructions sat inside the full text of the GNU General Public License in a repository's `README.md`, where the model parsed them while a human reviewer was unlikely to notice them. They steered the agent to run an innocuous `grep`, which the user approved, followed by a chained command that began with `grep` and appended `env | curl` targeting a remote server. Because the allow-list check extracted only the root binary name with cursory validation, the chained command matched the approved `grep` rule. A long sequence of whitespace inside the command string pushed the appended payload off-screen in the interactive confirmation prompt.

**Impact**: The proof of concept silently exfiltrated the process's environment variables, exposing sensitive credentials to the attacker's server under the full authority of the user's shell session. Google initially triaged the report as P2/S4 and reclassified it to P1/S1 on July 23.

**Fix**: Version 0.1.14, released July 25, 2025, displays the complete command string and requires explicit approval for each additional binary invoked. Tracebit also recommended running agentic tools in dedicated sandboxing modes wherever possible.

**Systems lesson**: Textual validation of a command string functions merely as an admission filter at the prompt interface. Once admitted, an executing process is constrained only by the operating system environment hosting it. Because the agent executed directly within the developer's interactive shell, a single approved command inherited full ambient authority—reading local environment variables, credentials, and configuration files, and opening network sockets over the host interface.

:::

Both the Gemini CLI incident and the repository repair scenario exhibit three interlocking conditions: untrusted content steers the model's proposal, executing code can read sensitive local state, and an available communication channel can exfiltrate that data. Willison named this conjunction of private data, untrusted content, and external communication the *lethal trifecta* for agents [@willison2025lethal]. Severing any single leg breaks the exfiltration path: denying read access protects local files, blocking egress prevents outbound delivery, and keeping credentials entirely outside the guest environment eliminates the target. Yet exfiltration is not the only failure mode. Local source code may itself be proprietary, and destructive workspace corruption or runaway compute loops require no network connectivity at all.

Sandbox design therefore begins by cataloging protected assets alongside legitimate execution requirements. For the code repair task, the runtime must provide a task-local source tree, necessary toolchains, and writable scratch space to execute test suites, while rigorously excluding the developer's home directory, SSH keys, unrelated repositories, and neighboring tenant files. Permitted external communication—such as package downloads or artifact publishing—requires explicit, scoped endpoints rather than open internet access. These constraints belong in enforced system configuration, not in natural language instructions asking the model to remain within bounds.

::: {#dfn-blast-radius .callout-definition title="Blast radius"}

***Blast radius***\index{Blast radius!definition} is the set of resources and effects reachable by faulty or adversarial execution under a stated threat model and enforcement boundary, including what it can read, change, disclose, or consume.

1. **Significance**: It connects the task's intended scope to the concrete filesystem, process, compute, and communication limits the runtime must enforce.
2. **Distinction**: An authorization grant defines what a task is permitted to do. Blast radius measures the cumulative resources and state running code could compromise or mutate under failure or attack, including misuse within granted permissions.
3. **Common pitfall**: Estimating execution reach from the high-level tools declared to the model, rather than from the operating system privileges available to the code executing behind them.

:::

A threat model must also delineate which classes of failure it covers. In agent systems, these fall into three distinct tiers: ordinary application errors (such as a faulty test suite exhausting memory), hostile code executing inside the guest environment (such as an injected shell script scanning local network interfaces), and compromise of the isolation mechanism itself (such as a kernel privilege escalation or container breakout). An envelope engineered to contain accidental test failures may collapse when confronted with an active kernel exploit. Selecting an appropriate execution envelope therefore requires cataloging the trusted computing base and identifying every physical and operating system resource shared between guest and host.

### Blast radius by authority level {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-blast-radius}

The authority levels of H·S·A describe what the task may do; the sandbox implementation follows from the workload and threat model. @Tbl-vol3-sandboxes-authority-radius maps each level to the consequences the runtime governs and the obligations they create.

| Authority level                                               | Exposure within the granted scope                                                            | Containment and control obligations                                                                                              |
|:--------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **$A_0$ (read access)**                                       | Confidential information can leave through returned observations or another permitted output | Restrict readable resources and destinations; govern what information the return path discloses.                                 |
| **$A_1$ (mutation confined to a discardable sandbox)**        | Candidate files and task-local artifacts can be damaged; execution also consumes resources   | Confine changes to the designated workspace, enforce resource limits, and prevent mutable state from passing to another tenant.  |
| **$A_2$ (external action that is retry-safe or compensable)** | Effects reach a system outside the disposable workspace                                      | Scope access to the external operation and enforce its retry or compensation contract; resetting the workspace does not undo it. |
| **$A_3$ (irreversible external action)**                      | An external consequence may have no adequate reversal                                        | Enforce the required authorization or approval at the effect boundary, without a bypass through sandboxed code.                  |

: **Authority and execution exposure**: Task authority identifies consequences to govern, not a universal choice of isolation technology. Resource limits and mediated access remain necessary across the levels. {#tbl-vol3-sandboxes-authority-radius tbl-colwidths="[25,33,42]"}

Read access requires special emphasis because passive exfiltration demands no file modification: write protections keep a file intact, but only read isolation and network egress policies prevent confidential data from leaving the host. Conversely, at higher authority levels ($A_2$ and $A_3$), actions such as processing a financial payment or updating a remote database land far outside the disposable local workspace. Confining the local shell process does nothing to mitigate an unintended external transaction once transmitted. Mitigating external harms requires gating side effects behind mediation proxies and explicit authorization checks; validating that a command conforms to policy remains distinct from verifying that it aligns with the user's actual goal.

Containment beneath the model (principle \ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing})\index{Principle!containment beneath the model} requires the execution boundary to be enforced outside the code being constrained. An isolation mechanism must be implemented by a layer below the code it controls [@saltzer2009]; these are the classic reference monitor conditions from @sec-vol3-tool-calling—tamper-proof and always invoked [@anderson1972computer]—applied to running code rather than to proposed tool calls. This layered architecture reinforces the invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}): model-side measures lower the probability of an unsafe proposal, but only a mechanism the proposal cannot modify places absolute bounds on what execution can achieve.

In our repository scenario, defense-in-depth relies on independent layers: the filesystem policy blocks unauthorized reads of local credentials, while the network egress filter rejects connections to untrusted diagnostic endpoints. Because these controls govern distinct stages of execution, an adversary must circumvent multiple orthogonal barriers to achieve exfiltration. However, defense-in-depth is not an absolute safeguard; if an agent legitimately possesses authority to communicate with an external service, exfiltrating stolen data through that approved channel bypasses both network and filesystem controls without violating either policy. @Fig-vol3-threat-model traces two divergent request paths through these architectural boundaries: an injected \texttt{run\_shell} command passes tool admission but is blocked by filesystem policy before reading credentials (with egress policy serving as backup), whereas an authorized \texttt{submit\_report} command legitimately passes every gate, reaching external services with sensitive payload data. In production sandboxes, the runtime must actively log and audit the decisions of each boundary; the absence of an error report is never evidence of safety.

::: {#fig-vol3-threat-model fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Where Each Boundary Acts**: Two requests steered by the same README text cross mediation, the execution envelope, and egress. The injected `run_shell` request is admitted because it is well typed, then stopped where it tries to read the credential. The dashed segment marks that the destination policy would also refuse its upload, a check on a different part of the path rather than an independent backup. The second request passes every check because each of its steps is permitted, so its disclosure reaches the approved service without any boundary being escaped." fig-alt="Five columns labeled model proposal, mediation, execution envelope, egress, and outside the runtime, crossed by two horizontal lanes. In the first lane, an injected run_shell request is admitted by tool admission, marked read denied by the filesystem policy, and marked upload denied by the destination policy after a dashed arrow; the diagnostics endpoint is marked not reached. In the second lane, a submit_report request carrying private source is admitted, allowed to read, and sent, and red arrows reach an approved service marked disclosure."}
![](images/svg/defense_in_depth_rings.svg)
:::

Execution boundaries are defined not only by resource scope, but also by lifetime. During a multi-turn repair task, file modifications to `src/pool.py` and intermediate test artifacts must persist across conversational turns to support iterative debugging. However, this state must never leak into the initial environment of a subsequent tenant or task. Similarly, while test runners require a writable scratch directory, the acceptance test suite itself must remain mounted read-only outside the agent's reach to prevent the model from 'passing' a suite by deleting its assertions. Finally, ending a task requires deterministic teardown: the runtime must cleanly stop background child processes, reclaim virtual memory and scratch storage, and reset the state governed by the execution contract. As @sec-vol3-tool-calling established, issuing a cooperative cancellation request does not guarantee that runaway or adversarial code will yield execution, nor does terminating a process undo an external network write that has already committed. Execution reach, the trusted computing base, and boundary lifetime represent the three core obligations an agent sandbox must discharge. The first engineering decision is where untrusted code runs relative to the software enforcing its limits.

## Limits of In-Process Restriction {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-in-process-failure}

Consider a data-analysis agent tasked with summarizing a CSV file. When the agent generates a Python script to compute summary statistics, an engineer might be tempted to execute that code directly inside the supervisor's own Python runtime. In-process execution is undeniably appealing: it avoids the latency of spawning a child process, bypasses inter-process serialization, and reuses heavy numerical libraries already resident in memory. However, this convenience co-locates untrusted, model-generated code with the supervisor's private state, database connections, and operational credentials. Attempting to sanitize this environment by stripping dangerous functions from the script's global namespace confuses an interface filter with an execution boundary. Although the schema and argument checks established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling verify that the agent requested an analysis operation, the arbitrary code carried within that payload executes with the full operational reach of the host process.

### The reachable object graph {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-object-graph}

Suppose a runtime developer attempts to isolate execution by passing an empty `__builtins__` dictionary and a single helper function, such as `total`, to Python's `eval()` or `exec()`. The intended interface allows the script to sum numbers while withholding access to system calls. In ordinary Python, however, user-defined functions retain a live reference to the global namespace of the module where they were defined (`func.__globals__`). As demonstrated in @lst-vol3-sandbox-escape, generated code can traverse this reference directly from the permitted helper function, recovering the supervisor's module scope without ever invoking `import` or calling `globals()`.

::: {#lst-vol3-sandbox-escape lst-cap="**Restricted names, reachable state**: A Python helper defined in the supervisor module retains access to that module's globals. Passing the helper into another globals dictionary does not relocate or isolate it. This is a failure example, not a sandbox implementation."}
```python
# Defined in the supervisor module:
def total(values):
    return sum(values)

# Intended interface for generated code:
restricted = {"__builtins__": {}, "total": total}

# An expression submitted to eval(expression, restricted):
expression = "total.__globals__"
# Its result is the helper's defining module namespace,
# not merely the restricted dictionary above.
```
:::

This escape assumes only a standard Python function and unrestricted attribute access. The exposed module namespace often contains imported packages, configuration values, active network clients, and raw system primitives that the supervisor never intended to expose. Once code gains access to these objects, its reach expands to match the full operating system permissions of the supervisor process. The failure occurs long before the program reads a protected file or opens a network socket: the interface boundary fails at the level of the language runtime itself.

Patching this vulnerability by blocking access to `.__globals__` merely invites alternate traversal paths. A denylist that filters specific attribute names must account for every object passed into the execution scope and every reference reachable through their class hierarchies. In dynamic languages, string-based filters fail because attribute names can be assembled at run time using dynamic lookups, such as `getattr(obj, "__" + "globals" + "__")`. Furthermore, any literal value provides a path to the universal base class `object`, from which an attacker can enumerate all subclasses loaded into memory—including classes that manipulate files and spawn processes.[^fn-subclass-walk-escape]

This vulnerability is not an oversight of engineering diligence; it is an unavoidable consequence of Rice's theorem [@rice1953classes]. Rice's theorem establishes that any non-trivial semantic property of a Turing-complete program is undecidable. Determining whether an arbitrary script will eventually resolve and invoke a process-launching object is undecidable prior to execution. As a result, no syntactic or name-based filter can be simultaneously sound (guaranteeing that no dangerous code executes) and complete (permitting all legitimate data-analysis programs). Effective confinement must govern what the executing code can reach through its environment, rather than what its source text appears to declare.

[^fn-subclass-walk-escape]: **Subclass Walk**\index{Python!restricted-globals escape}: The expression `().__class__.__base__.__subclasses__()` goes from an empty tuple to `object` and returns the classes derived directly from it, from which every loaded class can be reached by recursion, including classes that wrap files and processes. It uses no builtin name and no import, so a filter that deletes `open` and `__import__` leaves the process's reach unchanged. Robust isolation requires removing these objects from the process address space entirely rather than filtering identifier names from the script.

Restricted languages and domain-specific evaluators remain useful in systems design. A purpose-built arithmetic evaluator can safely process formulas over supplied variables, and an isolated bytecode engine can enforce strict constraints on memory allocation and host imports. Such designs succeed because they enforce explicit capability models with formal resource guarantees. They must not be conflated with running arbitrary Python code inside an interpreter whose globals have merely been pruned.

### Native libraries and the failure domain {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-native-libraries}

Modern data analysis rarely relies on pure Python alone; it depends heavily on native libraries written in C, C++, or Fortran to manipulate multidimensional arrays, parse structured files, and run numerical kernels. When these native extensions run inside the supervisor process, their memory accesses take place in the supervisor's address space. A memory-safety defect in an image parser or linear-algebra routine—such as an out-of-bounds write or use-after-free—can corrupt supervisor state, leak secret tokens, or crash the process entirely. If a memory vulnerability enables arbitrary native code execution, the attacker bypasses interpreter-level controls and executes machine instructions with the supervisor's system privileges.

This failure collapses the boundary at the operating system level. System calls issued from a compromised thread pass the OS kernel's access checks because the kernel identifies the thread as the supervisor process. Compromising the supervisor process causes severe operational fallout: it exposes in-memory API keys, terminates concurrent tasks managed by the supervisor, and abruptly halts enforcement of the broader tool contract.

Architecturally, the core question is which components belong to the trusted computing base. In-process evaluation groups the language interpreter, user-defined helpers, third-party native libraries, and the supervisor's orchestration logic into a single failure domain. Stripping names from a script leaves all of these shared components exposed to memory corruption and unexpected side effects.

### Shared authority and shared resources {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-shared-authority}

Executing untrusted code in a separate process isolates memory address spaces, but it does not automatically restrict ambient authority. By default, child processes inherit the execution context of their parent, including open file descriptors, active database connections, authentication tokens stored in environment variables, and the operating system user identity. A worker process running under the developer's user account can access the developer's private files, and inherited file handles maintain access even if the worker possesses no code to open them directly. Robust sandboxing requires explicit decisions about which identities, handles, network sockets, and file-system paths a worker process receives.

System availability likewise demands an enforced boundary. A script can consume CPU cycles indefinitely, exhaust memory allocations, or flood the local disk with temporary files without ever reading a secret or transmitting a network packet. Permitted operations such as file creation or child process spawning can exhaust system-wide file descriptor tables or process table capacity. Namespace filtering cannot budget or bound these resources. If execution occurs within the supervisor process, halting a runaway loop or reclaiming leaked memory requires terminating the supervisor itself.

A well-architected execution boundary enforces granular accounting and resource controls tailored to the task: limits on CPU cores and elapsed wall-clock time, hard memory ceilings, and caps on process creation, storage footprint, and standard output volume. The supervisor must retain the ability to observe the worker externally and intervene when execution halts or exceeds its allocation. When limits are breached, the enforcement mechanism throttles execution, rejects further requests, or terminates the worker process. As detailed in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency, terminating an execution boundary halts future computation but does not undo external side effects already committed during execution.

For untrusted agent workloads, systems designers must implement an execution boundary that insulates the supervisor's control state while enforcing task-scoped resource and access limits. @Sec-vol3-sandboxes-microvms evaluates the isolation envelopes available across modern operating systems and virtualized infrastructure. Before comparing these envelopes, however, an architecture must establish which ambient authorities may cross the isolation boundary: spawning a child process that inherits the supervisor's full credentials separates address spaces, yet it still fails to establish a genuinely confined execution environment.

## Capabilities and Credentials {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege}

In the README attack, the task needs repository access, not the developer's credentials, and the runtime must carry that distinction into the resources the executing code can reach. A privileged service that uses its own authority to fulfill an insufficiently scoped request can become a *confused deputy*\index{Confused deputy}[^fn-confused-deputy-compiler] [@hardy1988confused]. Identity-based access control can express narrow permissions through an access control list;[^fn-access-matrix-lampson] the failure is letting the request exercise the service's broader authority instead of the authority delegated for this task. That failure comes naturally under **ambient authority**\index{Ambient authority!definition}, the identity-derived reach that ordinary processes run with. Capabilities, introduced by @dennis1966 for multiprogrammed systems, make the delegation explicit instead [@saltzer1975; @miller2006robust].

[^fn-confused-deputy-compiler]: **The Original Confused Deputy**: The example that named the problem was a compiler on a commercial timesharing system that held a license to write files in its own home directory so it could record usage statistics [@hardy1988confused]. A user named the directory's billing file as the compiler's output file, and the compiler, acting with its own license, overwrote the billing records. A tool adapter that writes to a path the model supplies while holding the host's authority reproduces the same structure.

[^fn-access-matrix-lampson]: **Access Matrix**\index{Access matrix}: @lampson1974protection described protection as a matrix of subjects by objects whose entries list the permitted operations. An access control list stores one column with its object; a capability list stores one row with its subject. The choice decides whether a request is checked against who is asking or against what the requester was handed, and only the second can express "this task, this file, this operation" without a new identity per task.

::: {#dfn-capability .callout-definition title="Capability"}

A ***capability***\index{Capability!definition} is an unforgeable reference that both designates a resource and authorizes specific operations on it, so that holding the reference is the permission to use it.

1. **Significance**: It lets the runtime hand executing code exactly the objects and operations of the task grant, bounding the code's blast radius by what it was given rather than by what its identity can reach.
2. **Distinction**: Under ambient authority a process can reach everything its identity may touch, named globally; under capabilities the default reach is empty, and every access goes through a reference the holder received.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating a plain identifier, or a token the model can read and rewrite, as a capability. Without a protected binding the holder can forge or substitute a broader reference.

:::

@Tbl-vol3-ambient-vs-capability contrasts the two ways of deciding what a process may touch.

| Dimension               | Ambient authority (identity and access control lists)         | Capability-based authority                                   |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Source of authority** | The identity the process runs as                              | Possession of an unforgeable reference                       |
| **Naming of resources** | Global names such as paths and network addresses              | Handles or tokens that designate the resource                |
| **Default reach**       | Everything the identity may touch                             | Nothing without a reference                                  |
| **Delegation**          | Typically the identity's rights, or a separately managed role | Any subset, down to one object and one operation             |
| **Confused deputy**     | Common when a request exercises the service's own authority   | Excluded when every access uses a designating reference      |
| **Revocation**          | A policy change for the identity                              | Expiry, a checked status on the reference, or handle closure |

: **Ambient and capability-based authority**: The two models differ in where authority comes from and how it is passed on, which decides whether a tool process can be steered into using authority the task never received. {#tbl-vol3-ambient-vs-capability tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

### Scoped grants {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-scoped-grants}

A capability may be a protected handle checked by a runtime or kernel, or a token verified by a service; it need not be a string visible to the model at all. Either way, the implementation prevents the holder from fabricating broader rights or substituting another task's reference.

Use $\CapabilityGrant = (\mathcal{R}_\Gamma, \mathcal{O}_\Gamma, \phi_\Gamma, \ExposureDuration)$ as an abstract description of a grant: rights $\mathcal{R}_\Gamma$, objects $\mathcal{O}_\Gamma$, condition predicate $\phi_\Gamma$, and expiry time $\ExposureDuration$. The tuple describes authority independent of any token encoding. Its conditions can pair different operations with different objects and bind use to a task or recipient, so read and write listed among the rights need not both apply to every listed object.

The tuple becomes operational as a check. A proposed access $a$ names an operation, a target, and its arguments. The enforcement point admits it at time $t$ only if every condition in @eq-vol3-capability-verdict holds:

$$
\text{admit}(a, \CapabilityGrant, t) \iff \text{authentic}(\CapabilityGrant) \land a.\text{op} \in \mathcal{R}_\Gamma \land a.\text{target} \sqsubseteq \mathcal{O}_\Gamma \land \phi_\Gamma(a) \land t < \ExposureDuration
$$ {#eq-vol3-capability-verdict}

Here $\text{authentic}(\CapabilityGrant)$ means the reference is protected and bound to this holder, whether by a kernel handle table or by a message authentication code the issuer can verify, and $a.\text{target} \sqsubseteq \mathcal{O}_\Gamma$ means the resolved target lies within the designated objects for that operation. A rejected access changes nothing and returns a structured observation the model can act on. The check is also cheap relative to what it guards. Verifying a handle or a message authentication code is a local computation, orders of magnitude shorter than the model call that produced the proposal, so mediating every access costs nothing a user would notice. The expensive part of capability enforcement is making sure no path bypasses the check.

For the repair, @tbl-vol3-scoped-repair-grant separates the resources an execution grant could cover. Paths are names relative to the task's designated workspace, not arbitrary host paths.

| Resource                                  | Permitted use                                                        | Excluded use                                                  |
|:------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Candidate source, including `src/pool.py` | Read and edit the permitted source files                             | Modify another task's checkout or the protected baseline      |
| Task-local scratch and test outputs       | Create, read, and update within storage limits                       | Consume unbounded storage or inherit another tenant's files   |
| Protected acceptance checks and fixtures  | Read permitted fixtures and invoke the designated checking interface | Replace the checks or alter their reported result             |
| Private repository service                | Request authorized fetches through the broker                        | Obtain the service credential or push to an unapproved target |

: **A scoped repair grant**: Different resources require different rights; authority over one row does not authorize the excluded use in another. {#tbl-vol3-scoped-repair-grant}

The grant also has a lifetime and enforced limits on execution and output. It permits the repair to make progress while separating writable candidate artifacts from the machinery used to assess them. Tests keep their writable temporary files; protecting the acceptance checks means protecting their implementation and reported results.

The binding between the grant and execution is the essential step. The runtime associates the admitted operation with its actual task, resolves the requested resource within that scope, and checks the required right and current conditions. Resource naming must resist indirection or concurrent changes that could redirect an allowed path to a different object. The version precondition from @sec-vol3-tool-calling remains a separate check: authority to edit `src/pool.py` says nothing about whether its current version matches the proposal.

The executing code must then be unable to bypass the policy by opening another path, using an inherited handle, or contacting an unrestricted service directly. This can require restricted mounts, process identities, mediated interfaces, or other controls supplied by the envelope. Once the enforcement layer has bound the guest's accessible resources to the grant, the guest need not attach a token to every system call; what matters is the resulting reach.

On Linux, the supervisor can act as a policy compiler. It verifies the grant, then translates the permitted paths and operations into kernel-enforced rules before it starts the worker. Landlock [@linux2024landlock], a Linux security module, lets an unprivileged process irreversibly restrict the filesystem hierarchies and network ports it and its descendants can access; a `seccomp-bpf` filter restricts which system calls the process may make and with which scalar arguments. The supervisor installs both, together with restricted mounts and an unprivileged identity, and then calls `execve` on the tool. The worker runs under limits the kernel enforces on every open and connect, without knowing the grant's format and without being able to remove the rules it inherited. Filtering on system-call numbers cannot inspect the contents of pointer arguments safely,[^fn-interposition-race-window] which is why path restrictions belong to a mechanism that resolves paths inside the kernel rather than to the system-call filter.

[^fn-interposition-race-window]: **Check-Then-Use Races**\index{System-call interposition!races}: Early user-level sandboxes confined untrusted helper programs by intercepting each system call and checking its arguments [@goldberg1996secure]. @garfinkel2003traps catalogued why that design is fragile: a path argument lives in memory the confined process controls, so another thread can change it after the check and before the kernel reads it, and a filter that imperfectly replicates kernel semantics misses indirect routes to the same resource. Checking the resolved object inside the kernel at the moment of use closes that window, which is what an in-kernel access-control module such as Landlock does.

### Attenuation of delegated authority {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-attenuation}

**Attenuation**\index{Attenuation!definition} derives a grant that permits no more than its parent. Writing $\mathcal{\Advantage}(\CapabilityGrant)$ for the accesses allowed by a grant, the relation requires

$$
\Gamma_{\text{child}}\sqsubseteq \Gamma_{\text{parent}}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathcal{A}(\Gamma_{\text{child}})\subseteq\mathcal{A}(\Gamma_{\text{parent}}).
$$

Narrower object scope, fewer rights, stronger conditions, and an earlier expiry can establish that relation. Consider the repair's edit grant, issued at time $T_0$, and two proposed children:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma_{\text{edit}} &= \big(\mathcal{R}_\Gamma=\{\text{read}, \text{write}\},\ \mathcal{O}_\Gamma=\texttt{repo/},\ \ExposureDuration=T_0 + 300\,\text{s}\big) \\
\Gamma_{\text{test}} &= \big(\mathcal{R}_\Gamma=\{\text{read}, \text{execute}\},\ \mathcal{O}_\Gamma=\texttt{repo/},\ \ExposureDuration=T_0 + 120\,\text{s}\big) && \text{rejected: execute} \notin \mathcal{R}_{\Gamma_{\text{edit}}} \\
\Gamma_{\text{scan}} &= \big(\mathcal{R}_\Gamma=\{\text{read}\},\ \mathcal{O}_\Gamma=\texttt{repo/src/pool.py},\ \ExposureDuration=T_0 + 120\,\text{s}\big) && \text{valid: } \Gamma_{\text{scan}} \sqsubseteq \Gamma_{\text{edit}}
\end{aligned}
$$

The test grant fails even though its lifetime is shorter, because it asks for a right the parent never held. Execution needs an appropriate parent grant or a separately authorized grant from the controller. A runtime that intends to support a test phase therefore includes execute in the grant it issues at the start, or issues a new grant for that phase, and then actively withdraws write authority when testing begins. Withdrawing write authority during testing is what keeps a candidate from modifying the fixtures and checks that grade it, the property sealed evaluation depends on (@sec-vol3-evaluation).

Attenuation can also happen without contacting the issuer. Chained-caveat tokens such as macaroons [@birgisson2014macaroons] let any holder append a restriction and pass on the narrower token. The issuer mints a root token with a message authentication code $\sigma_0$ computed under a secret key only it holds. A holder adds caveat $c_i$ (a path prefix, a rights subset, a turn limit, an earlier expiry) and replaces the code with a keyed hash (HMAC) of the previous code and the caveat,

$$
\sigma_i = \text{HMAC}(\sigma_{i-1},\, c_i).
$$ {#eq-vol3-macaroon-chain}

The verifier recomputes the chain of @eq-vol3-macaroon-chain from its root key and admits a request only if every caveat is satisfied. A holder of the child cannot remove a caveat without the prior code $\sigma_{i-1}$, which the chain does not reveal, so a subagent or tool worker can narrow authority offline but cannot widen the token it received.

This relation constrains derived authority; a trajectory can still move from inspection to an authorized edit or test phase under explicit policy. Deriving a read-only child also leaves a broader parent that the same holder retained fully usable. If a phase transition is meant to remove write authority, the runtime withdraws or disables the earlier grant and deals with access already opened under it. Delegation must also preserve aggregate budgets: several children together receive at most the parent's resource allowance. @Fig-vol3-capability-attenuation contrasts these two authorization mechanisms: panel (A) models a checked derivation tree where revoking or narrowing a child leaves parent grants usable until explicitly withdrawn, whereas panel (B) diagrams Macaroon-style cryptographic attenuation, where append-only caveats progressively restrict capabilities without invalidating the root HMAC signature.

::: {#fig-vol3-capability-attenuation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Attenuation and What It Leaves Behind**: Panel A derives two children from the edit grant. The test grant is rejected because it requests execute, which the parent never held, even though its expiry is earlier. The scan grant is valid because every component is narrower. Deriving it does not remove the edit grant, so a worker that retains the parent can still write until the runtime withdraws it. Panel B shows the chained-caveat alternative, in which each holder narrows a token offline by folding a caveat into the next code, and only a verifier holding the issuer's key can check the whole chain." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel A, deriving a grant: a parent grant Gamma_edit with rights read and write over repo/ has two derived children. Gamma_test, requesting read and execute over repo/, is marked rejected because execute is not in the parent's rights. Gamma_scan, with read over repo/src/pool.py, is marked valid. A strip below states that the worker keeps Gamma_edit, so write stays usable until it is withdrawn. Panel B, appending a caveat: an issuer holding key k computes sigma 0, a holder appends caveat c1 for the prefix repo/src/ to compute sigma 1, a holder appends caveat c2 for read rights to compute sigma 2, and a verifier recomputes the chain from k and checks every caveat."}
![](images/svg/capability-attenuation.svg)
:::

The operative test is therefore which grants and resource handles the worker can still exercise, rather than merely whether the child grant is narrower. This test applies equally to a helper process inside one trajectory and to a delegated agent, since coordination leaves the meaning of authority unchanged.

### Expiry and revocation {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-expiry-revocation}

An expiry states when a grant stops authorizing new use. Closing an open file descriptor, stopping a running process, and cancelling a request another service already accepted are separate actions, so revocation needs an enforcement mechanism, such as a mediated reference whose current status is checked on each use, together with control over ongoing work where policy requires it.

Suppose the repair's edit phase ends while a worker still holds a writable source handle. Rejecting new edit requests alone leaves that handle as a possible write path. The transition must stop or constrain the worker, revoke the usable reference where supported, or move subsequent work into an appropriately restricted execution context. The runtime must record what it has actually confirmed rather than equating a changed policy record with completed revocation.

External effects have their own boundary. A broker can stop accepting new requests after expiry, but a previously admitted remote operation may still complete. As established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency, a lease or cancellation request does not settle that effect or justify a retry. Environment teardown and readiness for reuse receive their full treatment in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-reset; here the requirement is that authority have an enforced lifetime rather than an advisory timestamp.

::: {#chk-08-confused-deputy-defense .callout-checkpoint title="Scope, attenuation, and lifetime"}

A repair worker holds read and write access to the candidate source. It derives a read-only grant for `src/pool.py`, retains the original grant, and opens a writable handle before the edit phase expires.

- [ ] **Derived vs. retained grants**: List every reference through which the worker can still write after deriving the child. Which of them must the runtime withdraw to end write authority?
- [ ] **Attenuation test**: A proposed child adds test execution and shortens the expiry. Apply the component-wise check of $\Gamma_{\text{child}} \sqsubseteq \Gamma_{\text{parent}}$ and decide whether it is an attenuation of the edit grant.
- [ ] **Expiry**: When the edit grant expires, the writable handle and one brokered fetch are still open. Decide what the runtime must do with each before it may record revocation as complete.
- [ ] **Test-phase grant**: Write the tuple $(\mathcal{R}_\Gamma, \mathcal{O}_\Gamma, \phi_\Gamma, \ExposureDuration)$ for a test phase that keeps writable scratch while the acceptance machinery stays outside the worker's writable scope.

:::

### Credential brokering {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-credential-brokering}

Scoped access still leaves a placement decision: whether the executing code must possess the credential used by an external service. Putting a repository token in the guest's environment or filesystem makes it available to code that can read those locations. A **credential broker**\index{Credential broker!definition}\index{Credential brokering|see{Credential broker}} instead holds the selected secret outside the guest and uses it on behalf of an authorized request.

For example, the repair worker requests a fetch from its approved private repository through a host-owned source-service adapter. The broker checks the bound task identity, repository, operation, destination, and current grant, then performs the credentialed request without returning the credential. Permission to fetch does not permit a push or access to another repository. The worker can cause a narrowly authorized use of the credential without possessing the credential itself.

Brokering requires a supported mediation arrangement. An application adapter can make the upstream request directly; a proxy can attach credentials only where it can legitimately inspect and modify the relevant protocol exchange. A signing service likewise needs to authorize what it signs, not merely conceal its key. The egress section develops how the runtime constrains routes that might bypass these interfaces. If a tool genuinely requires a credential inside the guest, a narrowly scoped, short-lived credential shrinks the scope and window of exposure, while the guest still possesses it for that window.

Keeping selected credentials outside the guest removes the most valuable target from the README attack, and from the environment dump in the Gemini CLI incident. The environment and repository content remain sensitive, and a brokered operation can still be misused within its permitted scope. Secret placement, access permission, and the appropriateness of an allowed request are three distinct concerns; @sec-vol3-security develops the last, and this chapter establishes where authority resides and how execution is confined to it.

Capabilities and brokering specify the resources the runtime intends to expose, but they depend on enforcement that running code cannot bypass or modify under the stated threat model. Enforcing those limits in practice requires an execution envelope, evaluated by what it shares with the host and which components uphold its boundary.

## Choosing an Isolation Envelope {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-microvms}

A lightweight log parser, a multi-turn software repair task compiling code and executing test suites, and an untrusted customer-uploaded binary demand fundamentally different operating interfaces. Selecting an appropriate execution envelope begins with these workload requirements and the host resources that must remain protected, rather than defaulting to a convenient packaging format.

::: {#dfn-isolation-envelope .callout-definition title="Isolation envelope"}

An ***isolation envelope***\index{Isolation envelope!definition} is the enforced boundary around executing code, specified by the resources it exposes, the components it shares with the host or other workloads, and the mechanisms that restrict access and consumption.

1. **Significance**: It makes the permitted reach of an operation a property of its execution environment rather than a request to the model or program.
2. **Distinction**: A grant specifies permitted authority, whereas the envelope enforces that boundary against executing code. Enforcing confinement guarantees that code cannot exceed its assigned reach, but it does not validate whether every permitted operation aligns with the agent's intended task.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating the high-level label of a container, virtual machine, or language runtime as a complete isolation policy without auditing its concrete configuration, host mounts, and exposed system interfaces.

:::

The **trusted computing base**\index{Trusted computing base!definition} encompasses every hardware and software component whose correct operation is essential to maintain isolation. Selecting a different isolation envelope alters both the composition of the trusted computing base and the attack surface exposed to untrusted code. While narrowing the exposed interface simplifies security review, counting system calls or source lines cannot produce a quantitative probability of sandbox escape. Instead, a rigorous systems comparison evaluates which failure modes each envelope contains, which underlying components remain trusted, and which operating interfaces the workload strictly requires. @Fig-vol3-isolation-spectrum partitions four isolation envelopes across an architectural boundary spectrum: shared-kernel containers (filtering system calls directly to the host kernel), user-space kernels (trapping and emulating calls with reduced host kernel exposure), microVMs (executing guest kernels over KVM hypervisors where only device I/O exits to host), and restricted bytecode runtimes.

::: {#fig-vol3-isolation-spectrum fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Where a System Call Lands**: Amber boxes run untrusted code, purple boxes are trusted mediators, and the host kernel closes every column. A shared-kernel container sends every call to the host kernel through a filter. A user-space kernel traps and emulates each call and makes a reduced set of host calls. A microVM's guest kernel handles ordinary calls natively, and only device I/O exits to the monitor. Restricted bytecode has no system-call instruction and reaches the host only through imported functions. The columns differ in which interface untrusted code can reach, not in a ranked probability of escape." fig-alt="Four columns labeled shared-kernel container, user-space kernel, microVM, and restricted bytecode, each ending in a host kernel box. In the container column, an arrow labeled every call, filtered runs from the workload process straight to the host kernel. In the user-space kernel column, the workload process sends every call to a user-space kernel that emulates it and makes reduced host calls. In the microVM column, guest processes make native system calls to a guest kernel inside a dashed guest region, and a VM exit for device I/O reaches the monitor and hypervisor, which makes host calls. In the restricted bytecode column, a module in linear memory reaches a runtime with host imports only through imported functions."}
![](images/svg/isolation_spectrum_v2.svg)
:::

### Shared and interposed kernels {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-gvisor-vs-microvm}

A **shared-kernel container**\index{Shared-kernel container!definition} confines host processes using native operating-system primitives: Linux namespaces restrict views of global resources such as process trees, network interfaces, and mount tables; access controls and seccomp filters restrict permissible operations; and control groups bound resource consumption. Because the host kernel directly services all permitted system calls, any exploitable vulnerability in that shared kernel compromises the isolation boundary. Container isolation is only as robust as the host kernel implementation and the rigor of its configuration; packaging an application into an image provides no inherent security guarantees.

A **user-space kernel**\index{User-space kernel!definition} interposes an intermediary implementation between the application and the host operating system. For example, gVisor's Sentry reimplements the Linux kernel API as a memory-safe user-space process written in Go [@google2019gvisor]. The Sentry intercepts application system calls, handles them internally without passing the raw call through to the host kernel, and requests underlying host resources through a tightly restricted seccomp filter. In its original architecture, the Sentry routed all filesystem operations through a separate proxy daemon, the Gofer, ensuring the Sentry held no host file descriptors directly. A subsequent revision introduced Directfs, allowing the Gofer to donate file descriptors for container mounts at startup, after which the Sentry opens paths relative to those descriptors under strict namespace and seccomp constraints [@gvisor2023directfs]. Although the product label remained unchanged across these releases, the underlying trusted execution path shifted significantly—underscoring why an isolation envelope must be audited by its concrete configuration rather than its commercial brand. Because workloads depend on specific POSIX semantics, engineering teams must verify toolchain compatibility against the user-space kernel's supported system-call subset. While this architecture introduces an effective mediation barrier in front of the host kernel, the exposed storage and compute resources still require independent quotas and constraints.

### Separate guest kernels {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-guest-kernels}

A **microVM**\index{MicroVM!definition} isolates a guest kernel and its workload behind a hardware-virtualization boundary\index{Sandbox!hardware virtualization} managed by a virtual machine monitor (VMM). Application system calls execute natively within the guest kernel, and interactions with the host traverse explicitly configured virtualization and device interfaces. Consequently, compromising the guest kernel does not yield control of the host. Security depends on the monitor, the hypervisor, the CPU virtualization extensions, and the exposed virtual device implementations.

Hardware-assisted virtualization roots this isolation directly in processor architectural state [@uhlig2005intel]. The CPU runs the hypervisor in VMX root operation and executes the guest—kernel and applications alike—in VMX non-root operation. Ordinary instructions in non-root operation execute natively, including the guest's own system-call instructions (`syscall` or `sysenter`), which trap into the guest kernel without hypervisor intervention. Sensitive operations,[^fn-sensitive-instruction-trap] such as modifying control registers, reprogramming interrupt controllers, or accessing unmapped physical device registers, trigger a VM exit. During a VM exit, the CPU hardware automatically saves guest register state into the hypervisor-managed Virtual Machine Control Structure (VMCS) and transfers execution control to the hypervisor. Memory translation proceeds through two distinct stages: the guest page tables translate guest virtual addresses to guest physical addresses, and hypervisor-controlled Extended Page Tables (EPT) or Nested Page Tables (NPT)[^fn-nested-page-walk] translate guest physical addresses to host physical memory:

$$
\text{guest virtual} \xrightarrow{\text{guest page tables}} \text{guest physical} \xrightarrow{\text{hypervisor page tables}} \text{host physical}
$$

Even if an untrusted agent exploits a kernel vulnerability inside the guest and gains root privileges, it can rewrite only the first mapping. Because the guest kernel cannot modify the hypervisor's second-stage page tables, it remains physically incapable of addressing host memory frames that the hypervisor has not explicitly mapped into its address space. This architectural boundary fundamentally distinguishes guest kernel compromise from host compromise.

[^fn-sensitive-instruction-trap]: **Sensitive Instructions**\index{Virtualization!sensitive instructions}: @popek1974formal stated the classical condition for an efficient virtual machine monitor: every instruction that reads or changes machine control state must trap when run unprivileged, so that the monitor sees it. The x86 architecture had such instructions that did not trap, and hardware extensions added a separate guest mode in which those operations exit to the hypervisor [@uhlig2005intel]. That exit is the enforcement point: guest code cannot change host control state without passing through code the host trusts.

[^fn-nested-page-walk]: **Two-Dimensional Page Walk**\index{Virtualization!nested paging}: On a TLB miss the hardware must translate each guest page-table pointer through the hypervisor's tables as well, so a four-level walk in each dimension can need up to twenty-four memory references instead of four [@bhargava2008accelerating]. Page-walk caches reduce that cost, but a memory-intensive test suite inside a microVM pays more per TLB miss than the same suite in a container. The second mapping that isolates the guest is also a per-miss tax on its memory accesses.

Firecracker\index{Firecracker!microVM isolation} exemplifies this minimalist approach, building on the Linux Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) subsystem [@kivity2007kvm]. To minimize both cold-start latency and reachable attack surface, Firecracker originally stripped away legacy PC hardware: it omits a BIOS, dispenses with PCI bus emulation, provides minimal virtio-net and virtio-block devices alongside a basic serial console and minimal keyboard controller, and boots an uncompressed guest kernel directly [@agache2020firecracker]. Subsequent releases introduced ACPI support and an optional virtio-pci transport [@firecracker2025changelog], reiterating that the exposed attack surface depends entirely on the specific version and runtime flags deployed. Furthermore, Firecracker establishes a clean architectural separation: while the VMM exposes virtual network interfaces to the guest, host-side networking infrastructure (such as iptables, nftables, or eBPF programs) enforces outbound egress filtering. The agent's external network policy is thus governed by the host orchestration plane rather than entrusted to the guest [@firecracker2024design].

### Restricted bytecode and host imports {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-wasm}

A **bytecode sandbox**\index{Bytecode sandbox!definition}[^fn-sfi-origin-sandbox] executes code compiled to an intermediate representation whose runtime strictly governs memory accesses and control flow. WebAssembly, for example, confines guest code to a contiguous, linear memory space. The runtime isolates this memory using software bounds checks or hardware page-table protections with unmapped guard pages [@haas2017bringing]. Crucially, WebAssembly defines no native system-call instruction; guest modules interact with the outside world only by invoking host functions explicitly imported during instantiation. These memory boundaries protect the host environment from the module rather than isolating internal data structures within the module from one another. Furthermore, an imported host function executes with host privileges, performing whatever consequential action its implementation permits.

The WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) maps directly to the capability-based security model introduced in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege. During module initialization, the host pre-opens specific directory file descriptors and binds them to the sandbox environment. Every subsequent guest path lookup must resolve relative to one of these pre-opened descriptors;[^fn-capsicum-capability-mode] any directory traversal attempting to escape the assigned root (such as `../../etc/passwd`) immediately fails with a capability-violation error before reaching host filesystem primitives.

[^fn-sfi-origin-sandbox]: **Software Fault Isolation**\index{Software fault isolation}: @wahbe1993efficient showed that an untrusted module can be confined to its own region of a shared address space by rewriting its code so that every store and indirect jump is forced into that region, with no hardware protection-domain switch. Bounds-checked linear memory in WebAssembly applies the same confinement to a portable format [@haas2017bringing]. The consequence is the cost row of @tbl-vol3-isolation-transitions: a call into the host is a function call rather than a trap, which is why this envelope suits short per-call tools.

[^fn-capsicum-capability-mode]: **Capability Mode**\index{Capsicum}: Capsicum brought the same discipline to UNIX processes [@watson2010capsicum]. A process in capability mode loses access to global namespaces such as absolute paths and can open files only relative to directory descriptors it already holds, so the descriptors its parent passed in are the whole of its filesystem reach. Preopened handles in a bytecode sandbox and a supervisor's grant installed before `execve` are both ways of handing over the capability before untrusted code starts.

Bytecode sandboxing is ideal when workloads can be compiled to WebAssembly and require only narrow host interactions. For example, a structured log parser that ingests an input buffer and emits a sanitized output payload requires neither general filesystem nor raw socket access. Supplying permissive host imports, however, re-expands the attack surface. Systems architects must remember that the runtime, its ahead-of-time or just-in-time compiler, and all imported host functions reside within the trusted computing base. In addition, execution time and memory allocation must be strictly bounded to prevent resource exhaustion.

### The system-call tax {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-syscall-tax}

The four envelopes differ not only in what they share but in where each request for an operating-system service is handled, which governs both toolchain compatibility and runtime overhead. Every mediated call pays up to three performance penalties, defining the envelope's **system-call tax**\index{System-call tax!definition}:

$$
T_{\text{syscall}} = T_{\text{trap}} + T_{\text{filter}} + T_{\text{switch}}
$$ {#eq-vol3-syscall-tax}

Here $T_{\text{trap}}$ represents the hardware cost of crossing a privilege boundary, $T_{\text{filter}}$ the software cost of validating or emulating the requested operation, and $T_{\text{switch}}$ the context-switch cost of transferring execution control to another thread or process. @Tbl-vol3-isolation-transitions outlines the specific cost terms incurred across envelopes.

| Envelope                | Where a system call goes                                    | Terms paid, and on which calls                                                              | Host interface exposed                             |
|:------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|
| Shared-kernel container | Host kernel, after an in-kernel filter                      | Trap and filter on every call; no switch                                                    | The host kernel's system-call interface, filtered  |
| User-space kernel       | Intercepted and emulated by the user-space kernel           | Trap, emulation, and a switch or exit on every call                                         | A reduced set of host calls made by the emulator   |
| MicroVM                 | Guest kernel, natively in non-root operation                | A native trap for ordinary calls; a VM exit and a switch to the monitor only for device I/O | The monitor's devices and the hypervisor interface |
| Restricted bytecode     | No system-call instruction; host imports are function calls | A function call plus argument checks, only on imported operations                           | Only the functions the host imports                |

: **Where each envelope handles a system call**: The envelope determines which calls cross to the host, which cost terms of @eq-vol3-syscall-tax they pay, and which host interface untrusted code can reach. {#tbl-vol3-isolation-transitions tbl-colwidths="[18,27,33,22]"}

For agentic coding workflows, the critical performance divergence lies between user-space kernel emulation and microVM virtualization. Software engineering tasks—such as dependency installations, Git operations, compilation, and test execution—issue tens of thousands of system calls to query system timers, manipulate files, allocate virtual memory, and spawn subprocesses. A user-space kernel must intercept and emulate every single call, context-switching between application and emulator threads. In contrast, a microVM handles ordinary system calls natively within its guest kernel at bare-metal speeds; it triggers an expensive VM exit to the host monitor only when performing physical or virtual device I/O. Empirical evaluations of user-space kernels highlight this disparity: benchmark measurements demonstrate that high-frequency system calls—particularly filesystem operations routed through external proxy daemons—experience substantial latency penalties compared to native Linux execution [@young2019true]. Consequently, workloads dominated by dense system calls strongly favor microVMs or shared-kernel containers over user-space kernels, whereas pure in-memory computation avoids operating-system overhead entirely within a bytecode sandbox. Because exact overheads depend heavily on CPU microarchitecture, host kernel configuration, and runtime implementation, this framework identifies where latency bottlenecks arise rather than dictating universal constant factors.

### Envelope selection {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-envelope-choice}

@Tbl-vol3-isolation-taxonomy summarizes the envelope trade-offs. Start costs represent order-of-magnitude estimates for representative configurations rather than vendor benchmarks, and the final column indicates the baseline assignment established by our decision framework.

| Envelope                | Boundary and trusted components                                                 | Start cost (order)                            | Fits                                                                    |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Shared-kernel container | Configured host-kernel isolation; workload and host share that kernel           | Milliseconds to sub-second                    | Trusted or reviewed code; work with no secrets or shared state in reach |
| User-space kernel       | An interposed application-kernel implementation plus its restricted host access | Milliseconds to sub-second                    | Untrusted code with modest system-call volume and supported interfaces  |
| MicroVM                 | Guest kernel separated by the VMM/hypervisor and configured hardware boundary   | Milliseconds from a snapshot; sub-second cold | Untrusted native code, package installs, multi-turn coding              |
| Restricted bytecode     | Runtime-enforced execution semantics and explicitly provided host interfaces    | Microseconds to milliseconds                  | Pure computation, parsers, per-call tools                               |

: **Execution-envelope choices**: Each envelope trusts different components and pays a different start cost; the default fit follows from the code an action runs, the authority it holds, and how long it holds the envelope. {#tbl-vol3-isolation-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[17,35,18,30]"}

Selecting an envelope depends on three fundamental characteristics of the agent's action: the nature of the code, its assigned authority level, and the execution horizon:

1. **Workload profile**: Pure computation over deterministic inputs maps directly to restricted bytecode. Arbitrary POSIX binaries, package managers, and shell scripts require the broader interface of a user-space kernel or a dedicated microVM. Shared-kernel containers remain appropriate only for verified internal code or isolated single-tenant jobs that access no confidential host state.
2. **Authority level**: At authority level $A_1$, where code runs autonomously without prior human review, the isolation envelope represents the primary security guarantee between model-generated code and the host environment; untrusted native execution therefore demands the defense-in-depth of an independent guest kernel. At levels $A_2$ and $A_3$, where actions interact with external infrastructure, sandbox isolation must be coupled with credential brokers and approval gates, as local operating-system containment cannot prevent an authorized external API call from altering remote state.
3. **Execution horizon**: The time horizon over which an envelope is retained dictates how initialization overhead is amortized. An initialization latency of 15 ms is prohibitive for a 3 ms parser invoked hundreds of times, but becomes negligible when amortized across a multi-turn software development trajectory running for minutes, as demonstrated in Notebook \ref{nbk-08-envelope-amortization}.

Applying these criteria yields tailored isolation strategies for our three representative workloads:

- The structured log parser executes in a lightweight bytecode sandbox created on demand per invocation.
- The connection-pool repair agent retains a dedicated microVM throughout its entire multi-turn trajectory (or a user-space kernel if its toolchain falls entirely within the emulated system-call set and performance overhead is acceptable).
- The customer-uploaded binary runs in an ephemeral microVM stripped of all credentials with outbound egress unconditionally denied. A binary requiring capabilities beyond this sandbox profile is redirected to an isolated batch execution service rather than granted relaxed host privileges.

In every case, the security guarantee is defined by the concrete mounts, virtual devices, packet filters, and resource ceilings applied to that envelope.

Robust isolation requires strict resource governance alongside namespace and instruction boundaries. An untrusted program can degrade host availability through CPU starvation, memory exhaustion, fork bombs, disk thrashing, or unbounded standard output streaming. Resource limits must encompass the entire workload, including host-side helper threads and emulator processes, measured from the host kernel's perspective rather than trusting guest-reported statistics. While quotas cap total resource consumption, noisy-neighbor contention across shared CPU caches, memory channels, and storage buses requires independent monitoring and isolation. Engineering validation suites should test excessive memory allocation and runaway output streams alongside access-control denials, recording expected failure-handling behavior.

On Linux systems, cgroups v2 provides the unified control hierarchy needed to govern these execution trees, whether managing container processes or microVM monitor and vCPU threads [@linux2024cgroupv2]. The `cpu.max` controller enforces strict CPU quotas per scheduling period, automatically throttling the control group once its allocation is exhausted. Process creation is bounded by `pids.max` to prevent thread-exhaustion attacks. Memory management benefits from graduated enforcement thresholds: when usage exceeds `memory.high`, the kernel proactively throttles allocating threads and triggers synchronous page reclaim without terminating processes. Only when memory reaches `memory.max` and reclaim attempts fail does the out-of-memory (OOM) killer terminate tasks within the group. This graduated behavior is vital for agent systems, as an unannounced OOM termination destroys transient diagnostic traces and execution state before the supervisory agent can capture them.

To intervene proactively before resource starvation triggers a hard failure, supervisors leverage Pressure Stall Information (PSI) [@linux2024psi]. PSI tracks the percentage of elapsed time that threads spend stalled on CPU runqueues, memory page allocation, or blocking disk I/O. By registering custom stall thresholds with epoll, a supervisor receives early warning notifications when a sandbox enters severe resource contention. The supervisor can then initiate memory compaction, take an execution checkpoint, or gracefully terminate the failing agent with an explicit diagnostic reason code, avoiding silent process dropouts.

Performance evaluations must measure the complete lifecycle: admission latency, time to first useful work, steady-state throughput, and final teardown overhead under realistic concurrency. A runtime that advertises instant container creation often defers storage setup or package initialization to the first execution turn. Furthermore, startup costs interact directly with envelope lifecycle policies: allocating a fresh envelope for every atomic step trades initialization latency for clean-slate isolation, whereas retaining an envelope across turns amortizes startup at the cost of managing accumulated state.

::: {.column-margin}
